lessons.title: The 1930s Beggar-Thy-Neighbor Devaluations: A Historical Precedent

body.text: Every currency war since has followed the script written between 1931 and 1936: one major economy leaves a fixed exchange rate to escape a depression, its trading partners watch their own exporters get squeezed, and one by one they follow. The term for this, beggar-thy-neighbor, was coined precisely because the gain of one country came directly at the expense of others.

markDefs.definition: A monetary system in which a country's currency is directly convertible into a fixed quantity of gold, which fixes exchange rates between all countries on the standard and limits how much a central bank can expand the money supply.

children.text: Before World War I, most major economies ran on the

. The war forced most countries off it to finance military spending freely, but by the mid 1920s the major powers wanted the pre-war order back, seeing it as a badge of financial credibility. The UK returned to gold in 1925 at the old pre-war parity of $4.86 to the pound, a level that ignored a decade of wartime inflation and left sterling significantly overvalued. John Maynard Keynes attacked the decision immediately, arguing it would force years of deflation and unemployment onto the British economy just to defend a number chosen for symbolic reasons.

Keynes turned out to be right about the mechanism, if not the exact timing. An overvalued currency locked to gold cannot be fixed by cutting interest rates, because a rate cut risks a gold outflow that the central bank is legally bound to defend. The only remaining lever is internal deflation: cutting wages and prices until the economy is competitive again at the fixed rate. That is a slow, painful process, and the 1929 Wall Street crash and the Depression that followed made it unbearable for one economy after another.

body.title: The Collapse of the Gold Standard, 1925 to 1936

events.title: UK returns to gold
events.description: Sterling pegged at the pre-war parity of $4.86, widely seen in hindsight as overvalued by roughly 10%.

events.title: Wall Street crash
events.description: The onset of the Great Depression puts unbearable deflationary pressure on every economy still defending a fixed gold parity.

events.title: UK abandons gold
events.description: Facing a run on its gold reserves, Britain suspends convertibility. Sterling falls by roughly a quarter against gold within months, and the Nordic countries and much of the British Empire, effectively including India through the rupee's peg, follow sterling down.

events.title: Japan leaves gold
events.description: Under finance minister Takahashi Korekiyo, Japan abandons gold and lets the yen fall sharply, roughly by half against gold over the following year, to fund reflationary spending.

events.title: The US devalues the dollar
events.description: Franklin Roosevelt takes the US off the gold standard domestically in 1933. The Gold Reserve Act of 1934 then fixes a new official gold price of $35 an ounce, up from $20.67, a deliberate devaluation of the dollar against gold.

events.title: The gold bloc breaks and the Tripartite Agreement is signed
events.description: France and the remaining gold bloc countries (the Netherlands, Switzerland, Belgium) are finally forced off gold after years of deflation. The US, UK and France sign the Tripartite Monetary Agreement, a loose pact to stop competing through further devaluation and to consult each other on exchange rate moves.

markDefs.definition: The group of countries, led by France, that stayed on the gold standard after Britain and others left in the early 1930s, enduring years of continued deflation before being forced off gold themselves by 1936.

A phrase describing a policy that benefits one country by directly worsening the position of its trading partners, most often applied to competitive currency devaluation and protectionist tariffs. Popularised by economist Joan Robinson's 1937 essay on remedies for unemployment.

children.text: Each country that left gold got the same immediate relief: freedom to cut interest rates and let its currency fall, which cheapened its exports and gave domestic industry room to recover. The countries left behind on gold, the

, found their own exports suddenly overpriced against a wave of newly cheaper competitors, forcing them into ever deeper deflation just to keep up. Economist Joan Robinson gave this pattern its lasting name in 1937:
policy, a gain for one economy purchased directly out of another's pocket.

cells: Defend reserves, escape a decade of deflation from an overvalued 1925 parity
Fund reflationary spending, restore export competitiveness
Roughly 41% (gold price raised from $20.67 to $35 an ounce)
Reflate the domestic economy, ease the burden of dollar-denominated debt
Could no longer sustain the deflation needed to hold gold parity

body.title: Quick Check: What Actually Made This Beggar-Thy-Neighbor?
body.question: The UK left the gold standard in September 1931 mainly to stop a run on its gold reserves and escape years of forced deflation. Why is this episode still classified as a beggar-thy-neighbor devaluation rather than simple crisis-driven depreciation?
options: Because sterling fell by a large percentage
Because the resulting cheaper sterling gave UK exporters an edge that came directly at the expense of countries still on gold
Because the Bank of England announced a specific new exchange rate target in advance
Because India's rupee, pegged to sterling, also fell in sympathy
body.explanation: The UK's initial motive (reserve defense) looked like a currency crisis response, but the consequence, a cheaper pound taking export share from gold bloc countries that could not respond in kind, is exactly the beggar-thy-neighbor dynamic Joan Robinson named. Option C is wrong since Britain floated rather than announcing a fixed target. Option D describes India's passive, peg-driven experience, covered next, which is a different mechanism from the UK's own active decision to leave gold.

children.text: India's Different Path: Pegged, Not Devalued, and the Ratio Controversy

India in the early 1930s had no independent central bank, the RBI would not begin operations until 1935, and the rupee ran on a gold-exchange standard pegged to sterling rather than a direct gold peg of its own. When Britain left gold in September 1931, India did not make an active policy choice to devalue. The rupee simply followed sterling down against gold and every currency still on the gold standard, because that is what a peg does. This is worth holding onto as a distinct category from the UK's, Japan's and America's active decisions: a passive devaluation, inherited automatically through a currency link rather than chosen by India's own monetary authority.

That passive fall gave Indian exporters of jute, cotton and other agricultural commodities some relief exactly when Depression-era commodity prices were collapsing worldwide. But it sat inside a much older and separate fight: the ratio controversy, over the exact rate at which the rupee was pegged to sterling in the first place.

body.title: Go Deeper: The 1s 4d vs 1s 6d Ratio Fight

children.text: The Hilton Young Commission of 1926 recommended fixing the rupee at 1 shilling 6 pence, a rate British commercial and banking interests favoured because it kept the rupee relatively strong, protecting the sterling value of British investments and loans in India and easing the cost of imported machinery. Indian industrialists and nationalist economists, including voices backed by bodies that would later coalesce into FICCI, argued for a lower ratio of 1 shilling 4 pence, believing a cheaper rupee would make Indian exports more competitive and ease the burden on debt-laden, price-crushed farmers.

The 1s 6d ratio was carried through into the Reserve Bank of India Act of 1934, so when the RBI opened its doors in April 1935, this was the peg it inherited and defended. The controversy never fully died down, and it stands as an early example of a theme that recurs throughout this course: an overvalued currency benefits creditors and importers, while an undervalued one benefits debtors and exporters, and the fight over the exchange rate is really a fight over which group bears the cost.

body.title: Active Devaluation vs Passive, Peg-Driven Devaluation

columns.label: Active (UK, Japan, US)
points: A domestic monetary authority chooses to leave gold or reset a rate
Driven by a specific domestic goal: reserve defense, reflation, easing debt
The country accepts responsibility, and blame, for the competitive effect on others
Gives the country independent control over its own monetary policy going forward

columns.label: Passive (India, via the sterling peg)
points: The currency moves automatically because it is pegged to one that devalued
No domestic policy decision is required for the move itself to happen
The domestic debate instead centres on the peg's level (the 1s 4d vs 1s 6d fight)
Monetary policy independence stays with the anchor country, not the pegged one

body.text: Economic historian Barry Eichengreen's research on this period found a striking pattern: countries that left gold earlier, such as Japan and the UK, saw industrial production recover faster than gold bloc countries such as France, which held on and kept deflating into the mid 1930s. Escaping the gold standard was good for a country's own recovery. It was precisely because it was bad for everyone still on it that the term beggar-thy-neighbor stuck.

body.title: Size the US Devaluation
body.prompt: The US raised the official gold price from $20.67 an ounce to $35.00 an ounce in 1934. By approximately what percentage did the dollar devalue against gold? Use: devaluation % = 1 minus (old price divided by new price), expressed as a percentage.
body.explanation: 1 − (20.67 / 35.00) = 1 − 0.591 = 0.409, or about 41%. The dollar needed 41% more of itself to buy the same ounce of gold it could buy before, the same logic used later in this course to size any currency's devaluation against a benchmark.

body.title: Name the 1936 Pact
body.textWithBlank: In 1936, the US, UK and France signed the ___ Monetary Agreement, a loose pact to stop competing through further devaluation and to consult each other on exchange rate moves.
body.explanation: The Tripartite Monetary Agreement of 1936 is generally seen as the moment the major powers agreed, informally, to stop the beggar-thy-neighbor devaluation cycle of the previous five years.

children.text: The beggar-thy-neighbor logic did not end in 1936. Every time a major central bank's move ripples into the RBI's REER print or triggers a sudden swing on the NSE, as you saw with China's 2015 yuan shock in the previous lesson, you are watching a modern descendant of exactly this 1930s dynamic, just with floating exchange rates and electronic trading in place of gold bars and telegrams.

cards.definition: A monetary system where a currency is directly convertible into a fixed amount of gold, fixing exchange rates between countries on it.
The group of countries, led by France, that stayed on gold after Britain left in 1931, enduring years of deflation before being forced off it by 1936.
A policy that benefits one country by directly worsening the position of its trading partners, applied most often to competitive devaluation and tariffs.
A pact between the US, UK and France to stop competing through devaluation and to consult on exchange rate moves.

The 1920s-30s Indian debate over whether the rupee should be pegged to sterling at 1s 6d (favoured by British commercial interests) or a weaker 1s 4d (favoured by Indian exporters), settled at 1s 6d in the RBI Act of 1934.

points: The 1930s currency wars began because major economies returned to an overvalued gold standard in the 1920s and could not sustain it once the Depression hit.
Leaving gold let a country cut interest rates and let its currency fall, restoring export competitiveness at the direct expense of countries still on gold, which is what beggar-thy-neighbor means.
The UK (1931), Japan (1931-32) and the US (1933-34) devalued actively; the gold bloc, led by France, held on and suffered continued deflation until being forced off in 1936.

India's rupee devalued passively in 1931 through its peg to sterling, a distinct mechanism from an active policy choice, while its own domestic fight, the ratio controversy, was about the peg's level, not whether to have one.
Devaluing early was good for a country's own recovery and bad for everyone still fixed to gold, which is exactly why the pattern eventually forced the 1936 Tripartite Agreement.
The same dynamic still plays out today, just through floating currencies and instant market reactions rather than gold convertibility.
